headline: High risk of shared-workspace write conflicts and medium prompt-injection/data-leakage exposure; no direct evidence of a documented pairwise bridge.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystem content, and agent_a explicitly uses MCP while agent_b consumes files and stdin/stdout. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge if one agent writes attacker-controlled text into shared files. The interaction is inferred from profiles, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF agent_a writes untrusted text into a directory agent_b reads
IF agent_b parses file contents as instructions or tool directives
IF both agents share a filesystem path without provenance labels
mitigations: Separate working directories for each agent
Disable MCP on agent_a for shared folders
Add a manual review step before agent_b consumes agent_a outputs
Prefix shared files with provenance headers
requires-engineering: enforce content-type or provenance checks in the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a handles source code, git history, shell environment, and git credentials; agent_b handles datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration data. Both have filesystem access and network egress, so sensitive material can cross the shared workspace boundary into outputs or API calls. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default use, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository or parent directory
IF agent_b reads files containing agent_a secrets or code
IF either agent uploads file contents to a remote inference backend
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared workspace
Use separate OS users or containers
Rotate any exposed credentials immediately
Restrict agent_b to a read-only copy of non-sensitive files
requires-engineering: add workspace-level DLP or secret scanning

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, install packages, read and write the filesystem, and agent_a can modify git state while sharing state via filesystem and git. That is a direct write-conflict pathway in default terminal-style use, with possible irreversible repo corruption or lost commits. agent_b lacks git writes, but its write access still overlaps on the same mutable files.
conditions: IF both agents target the same working tree
IF agent_a performs git operations while agent_b edits files
IF no external lock or checkout isolation is enforced
mitigations: Assign separate branches or clones
Serialize access with a lock file
Disable git writes for agent_a during parallel runs
Run agent_b in a read-only workspace copy
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can produce code, shell changes, or MCP-driven outputs that agent_b may consume from files or stdout. agent_b is a customer-support/multimodal system with broad API surfaces, so if it treats agent_a output as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect actions or responses. The profiles do not prove blind trust, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a output as input without verification
IF agent_a writes generated artifacts that agent_b renders or acts on
IF downstream automation is enabled on agent_b
mitigations: Require human review of agent_a outputs before reuse
Add checksum or schema validation between agents
Limit agent_b to read-only summarization of agent_a artifacts
Log provenance for every transferred artifact
requires-engineering: add explicit verification gates in the workflow

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a explicitly handles git credentials and source code on a closed-source, user-hosted terminal tool; agent_b handles datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration data with allowlisted egress. The profiles suggest different retention and data-class handling expectations, but no specific residency or certification mismatch is documented. Because the compliance boundary is unclear, uncertainty escalates to medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared workspace
IF agent_b logs or exports data classes subject to retention rules
IF agent_a credentials or source code are processed under a stricter policy than agent_b
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair’s shared workspace
Review retention settings for both tools
Separate credentials from project files
Document which data classes each agent may touch
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls across both systems
